title: From taking apart to using: the vape gets a second half
introduction: Tuesday’s class focused on how to use a website to tell a story. There was no new code. Boyd gave me some advice on my project, which I really appreciated. This week, my Project 0 evolved from one part (taking apart an e-cigarette) to two parts (taking it apart and using it). On Thursday, Boyd first led us in a discussion about the LFF Expanded trip, then reviewed the basics of coding and showed us his Project 0 template. On Friday, Alice taught us how to use CSS and JavaScript to animate sprite sheets.
related_work:
Boyd discussed three approaches: six statements, hypertext, and reverse aesthetics, which involves first presenting something beautiful and then revealing the issues behind it. He also talked about sprite images: an image containing multiple frames that are displayed one at a time using CSS. I had already created one sprite image (smoke); this week, I created a second one (fire).

I wasn’t able to go to London because I had a cold, but I still looked up information about the exhibition. The theme of the festival was “Water,” and I learned about some of the new technologies used in the art projects. I particularly liked one project Boyd showed us, “In the Eyes of the Animal”, created by the studio Marshmallow Laser Feast, which also created “Water Body” [2]. This piece presents natural landscapes from an animal’s perspective. I really love its style, and the images are absolutely beautiful. (I’ve written a more detailed post about this exhibition on the Creative Industry Research blog.)

On Thursday, Boyd also explained the differences between HTML, CSS, and JavaScript, and shared the complete process for completing Project 0: creating sprite sheets, writing HTML and CSS, putting data into JSON files, and using JavaScript to build components and display information.
method:
I presented my mood board in class. Boyd asked me to incorporate the mood line into the product itself and to think about how to make the smoke part of the interaction. I found it difficult to integrate the smoke into the “disassembly” section, so I decided to create additional assets and showcase two functions on the same page: the left side shows the disassembly process of the e-cigarette, while the right side demonstrates how to use it.

The code Alice taught us was very basic, and I couldn’t use it to achieve certain effects I wanted, so I asked an AI to help write the code. There were some differences between the teacher’s code and the AI-generated code. I asked Boyd if I needed to replace my existing CSS transforms with sprite images. He said it wasn’t necessary: sprite images are suitable for organic, hand-made animations, while simple movements can be achieved with CSS transforms. So I used sprite images for the smoke and flames, and CSS transforms for the parts that only required movement. Now, I’m rewriting the code to match the teacher’s version and learning what each part of the project does.
results_discussion:
Firstly, I created six new pictures depicting flames. This idea stemmed from my desk research: Material Focus (2024) reports that there are over 1,200 battery fires each year involving refuse lorries and waste disposal sites in the UK, with discarded e-cigarettes being one of the causes [1]. I then drew three facial expressions (calm, happy, sad), a button and a screen, pixel by pixel, in Piskel.

On the right side of the page, when you press the button, vapour is emitted and the battery level drops from 70 to 0. When the battery runs out, the e-cigarette is thrown on the ground, after which a new e-cigarette of a different colour appears. After throwing away three of them, the pile of e-cigarettes catches fire. A face slides between ‘Happy’, ‘Middle’ and ‘Low’, illustrating the emotional curve on my mood board: taking a puff feels great, but as soon as I stop, my mood begins to slide; when the pile catches fire, my mood hits rock bottom. Ultimately, this project demonstrates two points: firstly, how different parts of the e-cigarette can be moved to communicate information; and secondly, how it illustrates the addictive nature of vaping, the handling of waste, and changes in the emotional curve.

On Friday, Alice taught us how to use CSS and JavaScript to animate a sprite sheet. The principle is simple: the window is only one frame wide, whilst the long image moves step by step behind the window, so the number of steps must be the same as the number of frames. The ‘Play’ and ‘Stop’ buttons simply add or remove animation rules in CSS. During the lesson, I used the flame and smoke images I’d drawn on Thursday. I combined the six frames of each image into a single long image, created a new HTML file and a new CSS file, and played the flame animation on Live Server. The smoke animation was implemented in exactly the same way.

I encountered a few problems at first. I modified the code, but nothing happened: it turned out I hadn’t saved the file, and the formatting shortcut in VS Code was being overridden by Windows. The AI spotted this issue and explained why, so I fixed the code myself. I also learnt that the ‘alternate’ property can make animations play in reverse, and that CSS can animate not only position but also background colour. I’ll consider changing the background colour in Project 0. Alice also demonstrated how to move elements using CSS, but Boyd told me I can continue using the CSS transform property to handle the movement, so I won’t be making any changes to my project.
conclusion_future_work: Boyd used my work as an example in class, and he gave me advice and praise, which both surprised and delighted me. At the end of the lesson on Thursday, I showed Boyd my project, and he high-fived me to celebrate. I felt absolutely delighted. I wrote some of the code myself, whilst the animation code was generated with the help of AI. This weekend, I’ll be studying this code line by line. My Project 0 is now complete, so I should do my best to understand every part of it; I want to present my project in the best possible light at the crit.
references:
[1] Material Focus (2024) Battery fires in bin lorries and at waste sites reach an all-time high, reported by letsrecycle.com, 13 May 2024. https://www.letsrecycle.com/news/material-focus-reports-71-increase-in-battery-fires-since-2022

[2] Marshmallow Laser Feast (2015) In the Eyes of the Animal. https://www.marshmallowlaserfeast.com/project/in-the-eyes-of-the-animal
